title: The Joel Test: 12 Steps to Better Code
creator: Joel Spolsky
summary: Written in 2000 and still the fastest way to judge a software team, this is a deliberately sloppy twelve-question test where each yes is worth a point. Do you use source control, can you make a build in one step, do you make daily builds, do you have a bug database, do you fix bugs before writing new code, do you have an up-to-date schedule, do you have a spec, do programmers have quiet working conditions, do you use the best tools money can buy, do you have testers, do new candidates write code during their interview, and do you do hallway usability testing. Spolsky argues that twelve is excellent, eleven is tolerable, and ten or below means serious problems. The value is in the explanations: each item comes with an argument about why teams skip it and what it costs them, and several of the questions were contrarian when written and are now industry defaults.

title: Things You Should Never Do, Part I
creator: Joel Spolsky
summary: Spolsky calls rewriting a codebase from scratch the single worst strategic mistake a software company can make, and uses Netscape as the case study: the decision to throw away and rebuild the browser cost the company years during which Internet Explorer took the market. The underlying argument is about what old code actually contains. Programmers look at inherited code and conclude it is a mess, but the ugly parts are usually bug fixes, each one representing a real problem found in the field, sometimes after hours of debugging. Rewriting throws away that accumulated knowledge and guarantees rediscovering the same bugs. He also attacks the intuition that reading code is harder than writing it, which is why every programmer's instinct is to start over, and argues that the honest alternative is incremental refactoring of the code you have.

title: Choose Boring Technology
creator: Dan McKinley
summary: McKinley, writing from his experience at Etsy, gives the argument behind a phrase that entered the industry vocabulary. The central device is innovation tokens: a company gets roughly three of them, and every choice of an exciting new technology spends one. The point is not that new technology is bad but that it is expensive in a way that is easy to underestimate, because a boring technology has known and well-documented failure modes while a new one has unknown ones you will discover in production. He contrasts the long tail of operational burden, monitoring, backups, upgrades, on-call knowledge, that each additional database or language adds against the narrow benefit that motivated adopting it. The essay then turns constructive, offering how to evaluate whether a new technology is worth a token, how to shrink the problem so existing tools solve it, and how to add technology carefully when it really is necessary.

title: The Best Code is No Code At All
creator: Jeff Atwood
summary: A short piece arguing that lines of code are a liability rather than an asset. Every line has to be read, understood, tested, debugged, and maintained by someone, possibly for years, so the programmer who solves a problem in fewer lines has done more work rather than less. Atwood contrasts the instinct to demonstrate effort through volume with the discipline of deleting, and points out that the most reliable code in any system is the code that was never written. He connects this to concrete practices: preferring existing libraries and platform features to bespoke implementations, being suspicious of frameworks and abstractions that exist to support code you could remove instead, and treating a large diff with fewer features as a warning. The tone is practical rather than dogmatic, and the argument holds up in an era where generating code has become nearly free and reading it has not.

title: Fast Software, the Best Software
creator: Craig Mod
summary: Mod makes the case that speed is the most valuable and least valued property of software. He means speed in both function and interface: no perceptible lag between wanting to manipulate something and it happening. Fast software integrates into a life, while slow software is opened reluctantly, and the difference compounds over years of daily use. He compares speed in software to generous margins in a printed book, something that makes you smile without knowing why, and illustrates with tools he actually uses, including a plain, oddly named notes application built on text files. The essay also argues that speed is a proxy readers use to judge engineering quality and care, that responsiveness changes what people are willing to do with a tool rather than merely how pleasant it is, and that most modern slowness is a choice made by teams who never measured what they were spending.

title: The Humble Programmer (EWD 340)
creator: Edsger W. Dijkstra
publication: ACM Turing Lecture 1972, E.W. Dijkstra Archive
summary: Dijkstra's 1972 Turing Award lecture, opening with his entry into a profession that barely existed, on the first spring morning of 1952, as he believes the first programmer in the Netherlands. He traces how hardware improved by orders of magnitude while the software crisis got worse, and argues this is not a paradox: more powerful machines make larger and more ambitious programs possible, and the limiting factor becomes the human capacity to understand what has been written. The central claim is that programming is difficult because our skulls are small, and that competent programming requires recognising this rather than being clever. From that he draws the recommendations he is remembered for, including structured programming, treating proof and program as things to develop together, choosing languages that reduce the space of possible mistakes, and abandoning the idea that debugging can substitute for thinking.

title: As We May Think
creator: Vannevar Bush
summary: Written as the Second World War ended by the man who had directed American scientific research during it, this essay asks what six thousand scientists should do next, and answers that they should make the accumulated store of human knowledge usable. Bush observes that the record of research has grown far beyond anyone's ability to consult it, and that the bottleneck is not storage but retrieval, because indexes are artificial and hierarchical while minds work by association. He then describes the memex, a desk in which an individual stores all their books, records, and communications, consulted with speed and flexibility, an enlarged intimate supplement to memory, with the ability to build permanent associative trails between documents that can be shared with others. The technology he imagines is microfilm and photocells, which dates the piece charmingly, but the hypertext idea arrived here first and influenced Engelbart and Nelson directly.

title: Information Management: A Proposal
creator: Tim Berners-Lee
summary: The document that started the web, written in March 1989 as an attempt to persuade CERN management that a global hypertext system was in the laboratory's interests. The problem it describes is mundane and universal: CERN was a large organisation with high staff turnover, information lived in people's heads and incompatible systems, and when someone left their knowledge left with them. Berners-Lee argues that hierarchical filing and keyword indexes both fail because real information forms a web of links rather than a tree, and proposes a linked information system with no central control, no fixed structure, and the ability to point at documents on remote machines regardless of their format. Notable details include a manager's comment that it was vague but exciting, and the fact that the only name he had for it then was Mesh; World Wide Web came a year later with the code.

title: The Web We Lost
creator: Anil Dash
summary: Written in 2012, before this had become a common complaint, Dash catalogues the capabilities the social web used to have and quietly gave up. Photos posted publicly could be reused and remixed under clear licences. Links between services worked because companies published open APIs and expected interoperation rather than lock-in. Publishing tools spoke standard formats, so your data could move. Discovery happened through links and blogrolls rather than an opaque feed ranking. His argument is not nostalgia for worse software, since he grants that the new products are more usable, but a point about incentives: each loss happened because a company found extraction more profitable than openness, and each was framed at the time as a minor product decision. He closes by arguing that the old web is recent enough to rebuild, and that younger users simply do not know it existed.

title: The Website Obesity Crisis
creator: Maciej Cegłowski
publication: idlewords.com (talk given at Web Directions, Sydney, 2015)
summary: A very funny talk with a serious complaint underneath it. Cegłowski is explicit that he has no problem with big image-heavy sites or video; his target is mostly-text pages that grow heavier every year, where an article of a few kilobytes of prose arrives wrapped in megabytes of scripts, trackers, and ads. He works through the causes in sections: fat ads and the surveillance infrastructure behind them, fat assets, and what he calls chickenshit minimalism, the fashion for pages that look austere while weighing enormous amounts because the visual simplicity is achieved with heavy frameworks and full-bleed imagery. He is equally hard on the proposed fixes, arguing that AMP and similar schemes solve a problem the industry created by handing more control to the companies that caused it. The conclusion is a defence of the plain web as the accessible, durable, and fast one.

title: The Mother of All Demos (1968)
creator: Douglas Engelbart
publication: YouTube (recording of the 1968 Fall Joint Computer Conference demonstration)
summary: In December 1968, Engelbart sat on a stage in San Francisco with a headset and a mouse and demonstrated, in one session, the mouse, hypertext links, real-time collaborative editing, video conferencing, windows, outlining, version control, and shared screens, running on a computer thirty miles away in Menlo Park with a staff supporting him over a live video link. Nothing like it existed, and much of it took decades to become ordinary. What makes the recording worth watching rather than reading about is the framing: Engelbart is not showing off features but arguing a thesis about augmenting human intellect, asking what an intellectual worker could do if a computer were responsive to their every action throughout the day. The pace is unhurried and the technology is visibly held together with effort, which makes the ambition clearer rather than less.

title: The Computer Revolution Hasn't Happened Yet
creator: Alan Kay
summary: Kay's 1997 OOPSLA keynote is famous for being both a great talk and a sustained insult to its audience, delivered cheerfully at eight in the morning to the largest room of programmers he had ever spoken to. His argument is that object orientation as practised has almost nothing to do with what he meant when he coined the term, which was about messaging and late binding between independent entities, modelled on biological cells and on the internet rather than on data structures with functions attached. From there he attacks the state of software generally: systems that cannot be changed while running, code that has grown by orders of magnitude without a corresponding increase in capability, and an industry that treats the current tools as the state of the art rather than as a primitive early stage. The Biological Metaphor section, and his demonstrations, are the core.

title: Aggregation Theory
creator: Ben Thompson
summary: The article that gave the industry its dominant framework for explaining why a handful of internet companies capture so much value. Thompson's claim is that the internet changed competition by making distribution and transaction costs approximately zero, which broke the old pattern where power came from controlling supply. Now the scarce resource is the customer relationship, so the winners are aggregators who own demand, commoditise their suppliers, and improve automatically as they grow, since more users attract more suppliers which attracts more users. He distinguishes aggregators from platforms and from traditional middlemen, works through Google, Facebook, Netflix, Uber, and Airbnb as instances differing mainly in how much supply they must own, and connects the idea to Christensen's conservation of attractive profits. The framework also explains, uncomfortably, why regulating these companies by conventional antitrust standards is difficult when consumers genuinely prefer them.

title: Tiktok's enshittification
creator: Cory Doctorow
summary: The post that coined a word now used everywhere, including by regulators. Doctorow describes a life cycle: platforms are first good to their users, then abuse users to make things better for business customers, then abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves, and then die. He argues this is close to inevitable given two conditions, the ease of silently changing how a platform allocates value and the structure of a two-sided market where a company sits between buyers and sellers holding each hostage to the other. Amazon's years of operating at a loss and TikTok's heat-seeking promotion of creators it later throttled are the worked examples, alongside Facebook's history with publishers. The wider point is about lock-in and switching costs, and the essay ends on what would have to change, particularly interoperability, for the cycle to be interrupted.

title: Reflections on Palantir
creator: Nabeel S. Qureshi
summary: A retrospective on eight years inside a company that was widely disliked during most of the author's time there and is now fashionable, which gives the piece an unusual vantage. Qureshi explains what the company actually did, as opposed to the spy-tech caricature or the dismissal as consulting masquerading as software, and describes the forward deployed engineer model in which technical people work on site inside a customer's operations for months, learning a business well enough to build for it. He is candid about the costs of that model and about what was strange internally: an unusual hiring bar and interview process, deliberate absence of titles, a culture of intense disagreement, and the way an intelligence-heavy monoculture both produced good work and made political misjudgements. There are also concrete lessons about enterprise software, institutional decay, and why so many alumni went on to found companies.
